outro.cta: Follow for business psychology that sells

scenes.vo: Nobody picked this option. And that's exactly why it worked.
scenes.visual: Three price cards; 100 dots pour in; the middle card stays at 0/100 with a red ring.

scenes.vo: In a classroom demo from his 2008 book, Dan Ariely showed a hundred MIT students three Economist offers.
scenes.visual: A crowd of 100 dots waits below; the three Economist offer cards pop in on the word.

scenes.vo: Look closely. Print alone costs the same as print plus web. Eighty four picked the bundle. Nobody picked print alone.
scenes.visual: The decoy card rings red; then the dots fly into the cards: 16 web, 0 print, 84 bundle glowing lime.

scenes.vo: Then he removed the useless option. A new group, same two prices. Only thirty two chose the bundle.
scenes.visual: The print-only card is stamped REMOVED and falls away; the dots re-flow to 68 web and 32 bundle.

scenes.vo: That's the decoy effect. Next to a worse deal at the same price, the bundle feels like getting web for free.
scenes.visual: A decoy vs target table: the decoy loses on every row; a lime 'Web free' sticker slams in.

scenes.vo: Picture a cinema menu. The medium is there to make the large look cheap.
scenes.visual: Three popcorn tubs rise; the large turns lime with a +₹30 pill. Labelled illustrative.

scenes.vo: But here's the honest part. In three point six million real wine purchases, decoys moved choices by about one percent.
scenes.visual: A wall of wine-bottle tiles lights up as a counter climbs to 3,600,000; a thin lime bar fills to about 1%.

scenes.vo: So use it carefully. Put a real, slightly worse option next to the plan you want to sell, and test it. Save this for your next pricing page.
scenes.visual: A pricing page: the decoy plan drops in beside Pro; Pro glows; an A/B test bar shows Pro's share rising (example numbers).
